# Results {#reses-peses}

## Population growth rates ($\lambda$)

The median population growth rate when excluding the effects of fishing ($\lambda_{dem}$) for the 77 stocks in this analysis was `r med.lambda.F0`, representing an innate capacity for population growth of approximately `r med.r.F0`% annually. Aggregating over years, the stock with highest median theoretical population growth rate was Atlantic cod in the Irish Sea (median $\lambda_{dem}$ = `r max.median.lam.nf`) and the lowest was pollock in the Gulf of Alaska (median $\lambda_{dem}$ = `r min.median.lam.nf`; Table \@ref(tab:tab-lambdas)).  When the effects of fishing were accounted for, the overall median population growth rate ($\lambda_{real}$) dropped to `r med.lambda.F`, which would correspond to overfishing by  `r -med.r.F`% annually (Figures \@ref(fig:lambda-bx-6-fig) and \@ref(fig:lambda-bx-other-fig)). 

The realized range of population growth rates was much narrower and the median $\lambda_{real}$ was below one more than 50% of the time in `r prop.usually.lt.1.fish`% of the stocks (Figures \@ref(fig:lambda-bx-6-fig) and \@ref(fig:lambda-bx-other-fig)). However, many of the stocks included in our analysis experienced infrequent large recruitment events that resulted in high $\lambda_{real}$ estimates (Figures \@ref(fig:lambda-bx-6-fig) and \@ref(fig:lambda-bx-other-fig)). For example, while the Gulf of Alaskan pollock has the lowest median $\lambda_{dem}$ (`r min.median.lam.nf`), it had a mean $\lambda_{dem}$ of `r mean.nf.of.min.median.lam.nf`, and when the effects of fishing are included this stock had the $8^{th}$ highest mean $\lambda_{real}$ (`r mean.fish.of.min.median.lam.nf`) in this analysis (Figures \@ref(fig:lambda-bx-6-fig) and \@ref(fig:lambda-bx-other-fig)). 

Mean $\lambda_{real}$ was lower than the median for just `r n.stocks-n.mn.higher.med.fish` of the `r n.stocks` stocks, and the mean $\lambda_{real}$ was less than one for `r num.mn.lambda.fish.lt.1` of the `r n.stocks` stocks, indicating that years of high population growth resulted in a net positive productivity for most stocks. The majority of the stocks with a mean $\lambda_{real}$ less than one were in the central or NW Atlantic (N = `r n.mn.lt.1.nw.ice`), and included `r n.cod.low.mn`  of the `r n.cod` Atlantic cod (*G. morhua*) stocks.

Several species are harvested throughout the north Atlantic, including two relatively large and long lived Gadidae species, Haddock (*Melanogrammus aeglefinus*) and Atlantic cod (*Gadus morhua*). These two species exhibited some of the highest variability in population growth rates both over time and among stocks (Figure \@ref(fig:lambda-bx-6-fig)). For both of these species, the variability of population growth rate declined as you moved from the eastern Atlantic to the western Atlantic (Figure \@ref(fig:lambda-sd-fig)). The pattern was most pronounced for Atlantic cod, with stocks in the eastern Atlantic rarely experience high values of $\lambda$ (Figures \@ref(fig:lambda-bx-6-fig) and \@ref(fig:lambda-sd-fig)). Pollock (*Pollachius virens*) is another Gadidae species with harvested stocks across the north Atlantic, the variability in $\lambda$ was lower for this species throughout it's range (Figures \@ref(fig:lambda-bx-6-fig) and \@ref(fig:lambda-sd-fig)). Atlantic herring (*Clupea harengus*) is a relatively small fast growing species found across the north Atlantic, there were no clear regional patterns in $\lambda$ for this species and the variability in the $\lambda$ were lower than the variability observed in several Atlatnic cod and haddock stocks.  

Two relatively short lived and fast growing species, (sand eel (*Ammodytes tobianus*) and Norway pout (*Trisopterus esmarkii*)) in the North Sea had exhibited high variability in $\lambda$, though this variability was smaller than what was observed in the Haddock and Atlantic cod $\lambda's$ stocks in this area (Figure \@ref(fig:lambda-bx-other-fig)). For the remainder of other stocks in this analysis, years in which the value of $\lambda_{dem}$ were elevated (e.g., above $\approx$ 1.5) were more rare, but no clear taxonomic or regional patterns were evident, with whiting (*Merlangus merlangus*) in the Celtic Sea, summer flounder (*Paralichthys dentatus*) and scup (*Stenotomus Chrysops*) in the western Atlantic, and the Gulf of Alaska pollock (*Gadus chalcogrammus*) stock in the Pacific Ocean all having moderate variability in $\lambda$ (Figure \@ref(fig:lambda-bx-other-fig)).

## Density Dependence

Overall both $\lambda_{dem}$ and $\lambda_{real}$ increased as abundance declined, the changes in the rate of population growth were more pronounced at low and high abundance levels; the relationship between $\lambda$ and the proportion of maximum abundance was relatively flat when abundance ranged between 40-70% of maximum (Figure \@ref(fig:dd-overall-plt)). The predicted population growth rate excluding the impacts of fishing ($\lambda_{dem}$) remained above one when the stocks approached their maximum observed abundance for more than `r pa.lam.nf.at.one`% of the stocks. However, when accounting for fishing mortality ($\lambda_{real}$), the modelled relationship dropped below one when the stock abundance exceeded approximately `r pa.lam.fish.at.one`% of the maximum abundance. At lower abundances, the model estimated population growth rate excluding fishing mortality ($\lambda_{dem}$) increased as abundance declined more slowly than realized population growth rates ($\lambda_{real}$). This is likely due to reductions in fishing mortality at low abundance, but since the fitted values did not overlap some fishing mortality remained even at very low abundance (Figure \@ref(fig:dd-overall-plt)). For the vast majority of stocks the lowest model estimated values of both $\lambda_{dem}$ (`r n.low.lam.at.max.nf` of `r n.stocks`) was found at the maximum abundance in the time series. However, two Atlantic cod stocks in the Northwest Atlantic had their lowest population growth rates observed at abundances markedly below the maximum. These Atlantic cod stocks seemed to have the least compensatory capacity at relative abundances near 40% of the maximum abundance.  

There was generally an increase in the variability of the $\lambda$ estimates as abundance declined, largely due to the increase in the magnitude of the maximum value of $\lambda$ (Figure \@ref(fig:dd-overall-plt)). While there was a consistent overall pattern, the estimated random effects demonstrated substantial variability among stocks in the strength of negative density dependence. For example, stocks in the western Atlantic (particularly Atlantic cod) and Alaska had some of the lowest $\lambda_{dem}$ estimates at low abundance, while several stocks in the North Sea (including Atlantic cod) had among the highest $\lambda_{dem}$ estimates  (Table \@ref(tab:tab-lambdas)).  Of the `r n.bl.40` stocks that declined below 40% of the maximum abundance, `r n.low.40.nf` had $\lambda_{dem}$ estimates < 1 at 40% of their maximum abundance; when the effects of fishing were included `r n.low.40.fish` of the stocks had $\lambda_{real}$  below 1 (Table \@ref(tab:tab-lambdas)).

## Recovery Potential

Lifetime reproductive success and generation length were estimated for each cohort in which data were available, population decline would be assured from lifetime reproductive rates consistently below 1. When excluding fishing mortality, the overall median lifetime reproductive success, (i.e., the number of females spawners per female spawner) was `r r0.med` (mean = `r r0.mn`; Figure \@ref(fig:r0-6-plt)). When fishing mortality was accounted for, the median reproductive success dropped to `r r0.med.fish` (mean = `r r0.mn.fish`). This difference between the mean and median for stocks experiencing exploitation, again highlighted the importance of occasional large reproductive events in sustaining these harvested stocks (Figure \@ref(fig:r0-6-plt)). For species found across the North Atlantic, the lifetime reproductive success when excluding fishing mortality tended to be higher in the east than the west, which again was most evident for the Atlantic cod stocks. While the reproductive potential of cohorts within a stock could be highly variable, there were no clear temporal trends in lifetime reproductive success (Figures \@ref(fig:r0-nf-ts-plt) and \@ref(fig:r0-fish-ts-plt)).

Generation length (calculated as the mean age of spawners contributing to a recruit cohort) was lower and tended to be less variable under fishing for all stocks (Figures \@ref(fig:gl-6-plt) and \@ref(fig:gl-other-plt)). There were again regional and interspecific patterns, for example, Atlantic herring is typically considered to be a short-lived species yet its generation length in the central and western Atlantic tended to be higher than the generation length of Atlantic cod and haddock in the eastern Atlantic (Figure \@ref(fig:gl-6-plt)). Similar to lifetime reproductive output there were no obvious temporal trends in the generation length among cohorts for the stocks in this analysis  (Figures \@ref(fig:gl-nf-ts-plt) and \@ref(fig:gl-fish-ts-plt)).

Based on simulated stock trajectories, the doubling time in the absence of fishing was relatively high for the majority of species (Figure \@ref(fig:dub-time-map)). Of the `r n.stocks` stocks in this analysis, `r n.dub.10` stocks were classified with a high recovery potential and this increased to `r n.stocks - n.not.dub.20` when including the stocks classified as having a moderate recovery potential after 20 years (Figure \@ref(fig:dub-ts)). Conversely, there were clear regional trends in stocks with low recovery potential. Of the `r n.not.dub.20` stocks in this analysis classified as having low recovery potential, `r n.alaska.slow` were in Alaska and `r n.nwa.slow` in NAFO Regions 2-4 in the western Atlantic. This meant that `r prop.slow.alaska`% and `r prop.slow.n24`% of assessed stocks in Alaska and NAFO Regions 2-4, respectively, were classified as having a low recovery potential. This contrasts to only `r n.nea.slow` of the `r n.nea` stocks in the eastern Atlantic classified with low recovery potential in the absence of fishing (Figure \@ref(fig:dub-time-map)).

The doubling time was influenced both by $\lambda_{dem}$ and the variability in $\lambda_{dem}$. Stocks with a median $\lambda_{dem} < 1$  were classified as having moderate to high recovery potential whenever the mean $\lambda_{dem}$ was $\gtrsim$ `r lam.rebuild.safe` or the standard deviation in $\lambda$ was $\gtrsim$ `r sd.rebuild.safe` (Figure \@ref(fig:dub-vs-sd)). Stocks with a median $\lambda_{dem}$ near 1 and with low variability tended to be stocks classified as having low recovery potential.
